c.tagline: Japan's crossroads with the world — atomic history, harbor views, and a hilly, exotic port.

taxi.fareNote: Ride-hailing apps (GO, DiDi) only dispatch licensed, metered taxis, not private cars; street and rank taxis are metered and easy to find.

hood_desc: The rebuilt area around Nagasaki Station, now the terminus of the Nishi Kyushu Shinkansen, with the Amu Plaza mall, new hotels and tram links in every direction. The most convenient, modern base for first-time visitors.

Shianbashi and the neighboring Doza and Kanko-dori streets form Nagasaki's main entertainment quarter — lantern-lit lanes packed with izakaya, bars and champon restaurants, next to the Hamanomachi shopping arcade. Best for nightlife and dining.

The historic hillside where Nagasaki met the outside world: Glover Garden's Western mansions, the Gothic Oura Church, the Dutch Slope and the reconstructed Dejima trading post sit above the harbor. The heart of the city's sightseeing.

Japan's oldest Chinatown, Shinchi, sits beside the covered Hamanomachi arcade — a compact grid of Chinese restaurants, ornate gates and shops that comes alive during the winter Lantern Festival. Great for street food and shopping in the center.
The residential slopes below Mount Inasa on the western harbor, famous for the ropeway up to one of Japan's finest night views. A quieter, view-rich base away from the downtown bustle.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.pay: The tram is a flat ¥140 (~$1) per ride, paid in cash or with a nationwide IC card (Suica/ICOCA) or the local nimoca — tap on boarding. A one-day tram pass is about ¥600; buses take the same IC cards.
transit.hours: Trams and city buses run roughly 6:00 AM to around 11:00 PM; after the last tram, taxis fill the gap.

train: Nagasaki Station (Nishi Kyushu Shinkansen / JR Kyushu)
ferry: Nagasaki Port (Ohato) — ferries to the Goto Islands, Iki and Gunkanjima tours

Bus to Ken-ei Bus Terminal (downtown), ~55 min

tip.r: Not customary; tipping is not expected in Japan.

food.name: Champon
food.desc: Thick wheat noodles in a milky pork-seafood broth piled with cabbage, squid and fish cake - Nagasaki's defining Chinese-Japanese hybrid bowl.

places.name: Shikairou
places.note: The restaurant that invented champon in 1899; 5th-floor dining room looks over the harbour.

places.name: Kouzanrou
places.note: Long-running Chinatown mainstay locals rate for the richest, most old-school broth.

places.name: Ringer Hut Nagasaki Chuo
places.note: Nagasaki-born chain, cheap and reliable if you want a quick bowl downtown.

food.name: Sara udon
food.desc: Crisp fried thin noodles under a glossy seafood-and-vegetable gravy; champon's crunchy sibling, eaten with a splash of Worcestershire sauce.

places.name: Kouzanrou
places.note: Both the thin crispy and soft thick noodle versions, done properly.

places.name: Shikairou
places.note: Same kitchen that created champon; the sara udon gravy is the benchmark.

places.name: Chuwa
places.note: Small, busy Chinatown spot popular with locals for lunch sets.

food.name: Turkish rice
food.desc: One plate of pilaf rice, spaghetti napolitan and a pork cutlet under curry or demi-glace sauce - a postwar Nagasaki cafe invention.

places.name: Tsuru-chan
places.note: Kyushu's oldest cafe, open since 1925, and the classic address for Turkish rice.

places.name: Cafe Olympic
places.note: Serves outsized versions with several sauce choices; a downtown institution.

places.name: Bistro Boa Vista
places.note: Western-style bistro take with a richer demi-glace, near the shopping arcade.

food.name: Castella
food.desc: Portuguese-descended honey sponge cake with a sugary crust on the base, sold by shops that have baked it in Nagasaki for centuries.

places.name: Fukusaya Main Shop
places.note: Baking castella since 1624; the yellow boxed cake is the souvenir everyone brings home.

places.name: Shooken Main Store
places.note: 1681 confectioner, also famous for its Dutch-style sweets and cafe seating.

places.name: Bunmeido Main Store
places.note: Big-name Nagasaki castella house with tidy gift boxes near Dejima.

food.name: Shippoku ryori
food.desc: A round-table banquet of Japanese, Chinese and European dishes shared from communal platters - Nagasaki's 400-year-old fusion feast.

places.name: Kagetsu
places.note: Former pleasure-quarter teahouse from 1642, now a designated historic site; book ahead.

places.name: Ichiriki
places.note: Serving shippoku since 1813 in tatami rooms; smaller two-person courses available.

places.name: Kouzanrou
places.note: More affordable shippoku-style course menus without the ryotei formality.

food.name: Chawanmushi and hatoshi
food.desc: Nagasaki's oversized savoury egg custard, and hatoshi - shrimp paste deep-fried between slices of bread, a Chinatown snack.

places.name: Yossou
places.note: Chawanmushi specialist since 1866; the bowl comes big enough to be a meal.

places.name: Kouzanrou
places.note: Reliable hatoshi and other Chinatown fried snacks alongside the noodles.

places.name: Shinchi Chinatown street stalls
places.note: Takeaway hatoshi, kakuni buns and sesame dango along the four gated streets.

food.name: Nagasaki milkshake
food.desc: Not a shake but a spoonable frozen dessert of shaved ice, condensed milk and egg, invented in the city's postwar cafes.

places.name: Tsuru-chan
places.note: Credited with creating the Nagasaki milkshake; still the reference version.

places.name: Cafe Olympic
places.note: Retro cafe serving a towering version year-round.

places.name: Seiyotei
places.note: Hillside cafe near Glover Garden, good for a shake with a harbour view.

food.name: Kyushu shochu and Nagasaki sake
food.desc: Barley and sweet-potato shochu from nearby Iki and Kyushu distilleries, plus crisp local sake, poured all over the nightlife quarter.

places.name: Shianbashi Yokocho
places.note: Multi-bar food hall in the entertainment district; easy hopping between small counters.

places.name: Ichiriki
places.note: Historic restaurant with a careful list of Nagasaki-prefecture sake to match the food.

places.name: Kagetsu
places.note: Sake service in the old teahouse rooms, best paired with a shippoku course.

landmarks: Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum and Hypocenter Park
Sobering exhibits and a stark black monolith at ground zero recount the August 9, 1945 bombing and the city's remarkable rebirth.
Nagasaki Peace Park
Seiji Kitamura's ten-meter Peace Statue points skyward to the bomb's threat and outward to eternal peace above fountains and international memorials.
Glover Garden
Hillside mansions of 19th-century Western merchants, including Japan's oldest Western-style house, overlook the harbor amid flowers and Madame Butterfly lore.
Ōura Cathedral
Japan's oldest surviving church, a white Gothic gem of 1864, witnessed the moving rediscovery of Nagasaki's hidden Christians and is a National Treasure.
Dejima
The meticulously reconstructed fan-shaped island trading post where Dutch merchants kept Japan's sole window to the West for over two centuries.
Mount Inasa Ropeway and Observatory
A cable car sweeps up 333 meters to what locals call a ten-million-dollar night view, among Japan's three finest cityscapes.
Hashima Island (Gunkanjima)
Boat tours circle and land on this hauntingly abandoned coal-mining island whose battleship silhouette and concrete ruins starred in Skyfall.
Megane-bashi (Spectacles Bridge)
Japan's oldest stone arch bridge, built in 1634, doubles into eyeglass-shaped reflections on the Nakashima River in the old town.
Sōfuku-ji Temple
A vermilion Ming-dynasty-style Chinese temple founded by Fujian traders in 1629, with two buildings ranked as National Treasures.
Shinchi Chinatown
Japan's oldest Chinatown glows with lanterns and steams with champon noodles, the heart of Nagasaki's centuries-old Chinese community.

train.note: Japan has no international trains. The Nishi Kyushu Shinkansen runs from Nagasaki to Takeo-Onsen in about 30 minutes, where the Relay Kamome limited express connects onward to Hakata (Fukuoka) - a through journey of roughly 1 hour 20 minutes. Because the line is not yet joined to the rest of the Shinkansen network, the change at Takeo-Onsen is compulsory but is timed cross-platform. Book JR Kyushu trains in English online, where reservations open 1 month ahead.

bus.note: No international buses run from Japan. Kyushu Kyuko and Nagasaki Bus operate express highway coaches from the Ken-ei Bus Terminal opposite Nagasaki Station to Fukuoka in about 2 hours 30 minutes, plus Kumamoto, Sasebo and Huis Ten Bosch, with overnight services to Osaka. Coaches to Fukuoka are cheaper than the train and about as fast; tickets are sold at the terminal counter and online in Japanese.

intl.to: Gunkanjima / Hashima (Japan) - landing tours from Nagasaki Port at Ohato
intl.op: several licensed tour operators (book through Nagasaki tour agencies; no single verified booking URL)

ferry.note: Nagasaki's ferries are all domestic. From Nagasaki Port at Ohato, Kyushu Shosen and Nomo Shosen run jetfoils and car ferries to the Goto Islands (about 1 hour 30 minutes by fast boat, 3 to 4 hours by ferry) and to Iki. Several operators run boat tours to Gunkanjima, the abandoned Battleship Island, but landings are cancelled in rough seas, so book early in your stay to allow a second attempt. Vehicles on the Goto boats should be reserved ahead in summer.

half.name: Gunkanjima (Hashima Island)
half.blurb: Boat tours reach the eerie abandoned coal-mining 'Battleship Island', a UNESCO site, in about 40 minutes from the harbor.

half.name: Unzen
half.blurb: A hot-spring resort among steaming volcanic 'hells' in Unzen-Amakusa National Park, about 1h30 away.

half.name: Huis Ten Bosch
half.blurb: A vast Dutch-themed park of canals, tulips and windmills near Sasebo, about 1h15 by train.

full.name: Goto Islands
full.blurb: Remote islands of hidden-Christian churches and empty beaches, reached by ferry or a short flight.

full.name: Shimabara
full.blurb: A castle town of samurai streets and spring-water canals beneath Mount Unzen, on the peninsula's east coast.
